title: Ketamine’s Role in Alleged Cornell Rape Highlights Flood of Psychoactive Drugs on Campus - Nautilus
gist: University of Virginia student health head Christopher P. Holstege warns that ketamine and spin-off designer drugs are flooding campuses and increasingly used in sexual assault, as highlighted by a Cornell civil lawsuit. Because most hospital urine screens cannot detect these substances, their true prevalence is unknown.

insights.claim: Ketamine and its emerging spin-off versions are part of a wave of new and evolving designer drugs entering the United States and other countries.
insights.speaker: Christopher P. Holstege
insights.so_what: Rising designer-drug prevalence signals demand for broader toxicology testing and campus health services.

insights.claim: Christopher Holstege, who heads student health at the University of Virginia, says psychoactive substances such as ketamine pose a growing danger to university students' health and safety.
insights.speaker: Christopher P. Holstege
insights.so_what: Points to growing liability and safety pressure on universities.

insights.claim: Most hospitals cannot detect ketamine and similar new drugs on standard urine drug screens, so how widely they are used remains unknown.
insights.speaker: Christopher P. Holstege
insights.so_what: A detection gap suggests a market need for expanded drug-screening diagnostics.

insights.claim: Ketamine and other drugs are increasingly reported as agents in sexual assault, whether taken voluntarily, under pressure, or administered covertly.
insights.speaker: Christopher P. Holstege
insights.so_what: Raises legal and institutional risk for universities and Greek organizations.

insights.claim: A former Cornell student filed a civil lawsuit in September 2026 alleging seven fraternity members raped her at a party after pressuring her to take ketamine.
insights.speaker: Christopher P. Holstege
insights.so_what: Litigation exposure for universities and fraternities over campus drug-facilitated assault.
